title: Sharp Quantum Capacity Thresholds: Exponential Strong Converses for Degradable and Antidegradable Channels
authors: Tulja Varun Kondra, Raphael Brinster, Hermann Kampermann, Dagmar Bruß, Nikolai Wyderka
abstract: The quantum capacity of a noisy channel quantifies the maximum rate at which quantum information can be transmitted reliably. For general channels, its evaluation requires an optimization over arbitrarily many channel uses. Degradable channels form a central exception: their capacity is given by the single-letter coherent information, while antidegradable channels have zero capacity. Nevertheless, even for these fundamental classes, it has remained open whether communication above capacity becomes possible when a fixed non-maximal error is tolerated. Here we resolve this problem by proving an exponential strong converse for every finite-dimensional degradable and antidegradable channel: at any rate above capacity, the fidelity of every coding scheme decays exponentially with the number of channel uses. As an immediate consequence, we establish the first all-code exponential strong converse for the quantum erasure channel throughout its full parameter range, strengthening previous results that applied only to almost all codes. We also show that exponential strong-converse bounds are preserved under receiver post-processing. This yields efficiently computable semidefinite-programming bounds for arbitrary finite-dimensional channels, improved bounds for Pauli channels, and an exact exponential strong converse for a nondegradable multilevel amplitude-damping family.
summary: This paper establishes rigorous, all-code exponential strong converse theorems for quantum channels, particularly focusing on degradable and antidegradable types. By proving that rates exceeding capacity result in exponentially decaying fidelity, it resolves long-standing open problems in quantum information theory. The methods involve sophisticated mathematical tools from operator theory and polynomial approximation.
main_problem: The central problem is establishing strong converse theorems for quantum channels, specifically determining if communication above the channel's quantum capacity remains possible when a fixed non-maximal error is tolerated.
main_result: The authors prove an all-code exponential strong converse for finite-dimensional degradable and antidegradable channels, showing that rates above capacity lead to exponentially decaying fidelity.
method: The proof employs advanced techniques involving the Choi-Jamiołkowski correspondence, constructing weight matrices from multilinear polynomials, and bounding operator norms related to channel placements.
model_or_system: The study focuses on general noisy quantum channels ($N: A' 	o B$), with specific attention paid to degradable (where capacity is single-letter) and antidegradable channels. The analysis uses Bell-target schemes for encoding.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F_n$) of the coding scheme, which decays exponentially with the number of channel uses ($n$).
important_parameters: The rate $r$ relative to the quantum capacity $Q(N)$, and the dimensionality parameters of the channels.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on bounding operator norms using polynomial approximations (e.g., approximating $	ext{NOR}_n$) and assuming specific structures for channel extensions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the definitions of degradable/antidegradable channels and the use of a symmetric two-output extension ($e_N$) to generate overlapping placements $\{P_x\}$ central to the argument.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the strong converse problem, then developing technical tools (like bounding $\lVert \mathbf{A} Vert_\infty$ using weight matrices derived from polynomial approximations), and finally applying these tools sequentially to prove the exponential strong converse for antidegradable channels, followed by degradable channels.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental, sharp bounds on quantum communication limits that are crucial for understanding the ultimate performance thresholds of any quantum information processing protocol.
